Respiratory trials conducted on the Mountain cuscus (Phalanger carmelitae) under standard laboratory conditions reveal a maximum resting metabolic rate of 534.9 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 534.9 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. All metabolic measurements were recorded at a stable body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], a value consistent with the typical thermoneutral zone for arboreal marsupials of comparable body size. The moderately low basal metabolism of this species, relative to eutherian mammals of similar mass, likely reflects an adaptive energetic strategy linked to a folivorous diet dominated by leaves and unripe fruits, which are often low in readily assimilable nutrients and require prolonged gut retention. The oxygen consumption rate, measured via open-flow respirometry in post-absorptive, resting individuals during their inactive phase, aligns with the general marsupial pattern of reduced maintenance costs and suggests that P. carmelitae operates under a relatively constrained daily energy budget, a feature that has significant implications for its life history scheduling and reproductive output in the montane forests of New Guinea.

Female Mountain cuscus reach an ultimate adult body mass of approximately 2500 grams [Wwi = approximately 2500 grams], with published accounts typically reporting a range between 1.7 and 2.6 kilograms, placing them among the mid-sized members of the genus Phalanger. This adult mass is attained only after a prolonged period of somatic growth, and the substantial size of the female has direct consequences for the energetics of reproduction. In stark contrast, neonates emerge after a remarkably brief gestation and are extremely altricial, weighing a mere 0.9 grams [Wwb = 0.9 grams] at birth. This neonatal mass, estimated from data on the closely related spotted cuscus (Spilocuscus maculatus), is among the smallest relative to maternal mass recorded for any arboreal marsupial, highlighting the extreme altriciality characteristic of the family Phalangeridae. The tiny newborn must immediately crawl to the pouch and attach to a teat, where it will undergo the majority of its morphological development during an extended period of lactation dependency.

The reproductive biology of the Mountain cuscus is characterized by a very slow pace of life, typical of many tropical arboreal mammals. Under the thermal conditions that define its normal physiological functioning at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], females produce a maximum of one pup per litter [N_R_i = one pup per litter] and, under optimal field conditions, may yield only a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year]. This extremely conservative annual reproductive output reflects the considerable maternal investment required to rear a single, slowly developing offspring through a prolonged period of pouch life and subsequent lactation. The gestation period itself is estimated at 17 days [tg = 17 days] at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], a figure derived from the well-studied common brushtail possum (Trichosurus vulpecula) and considered representative for phalangerids given the uniformity of their placental and embryonic development. This short gestation is followed by a much longer interval of pouch residency and nutritional dependence, during which the altricial neonate completes organogenesis and gains the capacity for thermoregulation.

A suite of important developmental milestones further illustrates the slow life history of Phalanger carmelitae when examined at a stable core temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. The time since birth at weaning, marking the end of nutritional dependency on maternal milk, is estimated at 204 days [tx = 204 days], a value extrapolated from the comparative developmental trajectory of Trichosurus vulpecula and consistent with the gradual transition to a solid-food diet observed in captive phalangerids. at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]Weaned juveniles then enter a prolonged sub-adult phase characterized by continued somatic growth and behavioral maturation. Puberty is not attained until approximately 222 days after birth [tp = approximately 222 days after birth], based on the model provided by Spilocuscus maculatus, meaning that young cuscuses are not reproductively competent until well into their secon at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]d year of life. This substantial delay in the attainment of sexual maturity relative to the weaning age is a classic signature of a slow-paced life history, allowing young animals to acquire sufficient body reserves and foraging skills before committing resources to reproduction.

Longevity records for the Mountain cuscus, again informed by comparative data from Spilocuscus maculatus, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 17 years [am = approximately 17 years] under optimal captive conditions, a duration that is remarkably long for a mammal of at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C] its body size. When expressed in absolute daily terms, this lifespan reaches approximately 6205 days [am = approximately 6205 days], and this physiological activity is sustained at a stable core temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. Among sympatric Phalanger species, this combination of extreme longevity and delayed pubertal onset firmly positions P. carmelitae as a slow strategist on the fast-slow continuum of mammalian life histories, underscoring a life history evolution shaped by stable montane forest environments where low extrinsic adult mortality prevails.
